newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - U.S. housing starts seen slowing in Aug.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.S. housing starts seen slowing in Aug.

text.p: Growth in U.S. housing starts probably slowed for a fourth straight month in August as steep interest rates continued to hurt demand, economists said.
But healthy gains in personal income and employment have helped housing starts overall remain buoyant at high levels, they said.

"Our view is that the home-building sector is being slightly undermined by the rise in long-term interest rates, but it's basically leveling off at a pretty healthy pace," said Dana Johnson at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc.
"Housing starts are basically at a standoff between income and employment growth and higher long-term interest rates," Johnson, who is head of market analysis, added.
The Commerce Department will release August housing starts on Thursday, September 19, at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
Economists polled by Reuters on average expect starts to slip to 1.445 million compared to 1.455 million in July.

Housing starts posted a 1.488 million average pace in the second quarter, an unsustainably high level given that interest rates have been trending up, said David Seiders, chief economist at the National Association of Homebuilders.
"Fundamentally, interest rates are catching up with the housing sector," Seiders said. "We've had a fairly decisive increase in long-term rates since early this year."
The association's Housing Market Index dropped three points to 57 in August from 60 in July, reflecting dampening sentiment in the housing market, he said.
Housing starts peaked at 1.514 million in February this year, as buyers rushed to lock in low mortgage rates.
In August the rate on the conventional 30-year fixed rate mortgage was 8.0 percent compared with 7.03 percent in January, according to the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp.
"There's always a lag in the effect from higher interest rates," said Mary Dennis, senior economist at Merrill Lynch and Co Inc. "We're looking for a little decline in single-family starts."
Single-family starts fell to a seasonally adjusted 1.133 million in July from a revised 1.201 million in June, the biggest monthly decrease since Jauuary 1995.
Multiple-family starts rose to 322,000 in July from a revised 273,000 in June.
Dennis said the "wealth effect" from strong gains in U.S. stock prices was helping to undergird housing starts.
"Right now asset growth and household net worth are still growing at a remarkably strong pace," she said.
Strong consumer confidence and a drop in the U.S. jobless rate in August to 5.1 percent -- the lowest level since March 1989 -- has helped fuel demand for housing, analysts said.

"People feel they can make this kind of investment and that they won't be unemployed soon after they take out their mortgages," said Carol Stone, senior economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.
